newsitem.title: USA: Lawyers in Exxon case seek $1 billion in fees.
newsitem.headline: Lawyers in Exxon case seek $1 billion in fees.

text.p: Plaintiffs' attorneys in the Exxon Valdez oil spill case on Tuesday requested about $1 billion in fees, proposing that the remaining $4 billion in damages be divided among some 32,000 claimants.

In a filing in U.S. District Court, the attorneys requested 20 percent of the punitive damages award plus $30 million in out-of-pocket expenses since the litigation began, and they outlined a plan for distributing the money.
Exxon Corp. has appealed the 1994 jury award, but Brian O'Neill, lead trial counsel for the plaintiffs, said at a news conference he was confident it would be upheld.

The court filing came almost eight years to the day after the Exxon Valdez tanker ran aground on Bligh Reef in Prince William Sound, dumping 11 million gallons of crude oil in the nation's worst oil spill.
The jury in the federal civil trial, which found Exxon and ship captain Joseph Hazelwood guilty of recklessness, also awarded $286 million in compensatory damages.

Last June U.S. District Judge Russel Holland approved a plan that allocated 78 percent of the punitive award to oiled fisheries, 2 percent to unoiled fisheries, 2 percent to municipalities and 16 percent to Alaska Natives, processors, private businesses and others.

The distribution plan identifies more than three dozen individual fisheries in Prince William Sound, Kodiak, Cook Inlet and Chignik, plus area businesses, cannery workers, municipalities and others affected by the spill.
It lays out specific qualifications for claimants within each group and how the distribution takes place. It takes into account lost fish, lost fish prices and devaluation of permits and vessels.

Formulas vary by fisheries, taking into account how the fisheries were operated and impacted, O'Neill said. Dave Oesting, co-counsel for the plaintiffs, said that although $5 billion was a huge sum, it was not a lot to divide among 32,000 parties.
"This is not a situation where any one individual is going to reap a huge windfall or even a windfall of any sort, simply because of the magnitude of the disaster wrought by the oil spill," he said.
Once Holland gives preliminary approval to the plan, it will be sent to plaintiffs.
Oesting predicted a final hearing in late July or early August. He said attorneys collectively had hundreds of millions of hours of work invested in the case.
